titleStmt.title: Interview with Norman C. Adams, 7 October 2005
titleStmt.author: Sue Paul and Joe Strickland [transcriber]

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Norman C. Adams was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.head: Interview with Norman C. Adams [7 October 2005]

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Today is October 7th, 2005, and we're at the Warhawk Air Museum conducting a Veterans History Project interview in conjunction the Library of Congress. Today we will be interviewing Mr. Norman C. Adams. Welcome to the Warhawk Air Museum, sir.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Also present in the room is Mr. Al Mascia (ph) who will be doing the filming. Sir, could you please tell us the date that you were born and where you were born.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: On [redacted]. San Bernardino, California.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And could you give us your current address.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: [redacted].

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Sir, could you tell us which war, or wars, that you served in and the division of the military.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I was in the Army Air Corps in World War II, the Eighth Air Force. And after -- I stayed in the service through the Vietnam and Korean War and served in the Fifteenth Air Force and the Eighth Air Force after World War II until, I retired in June of 1967.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Well, thank you very much. And we appreciate your coming here to let us do this interview. Norm, you were born in [redacted] in San Bernardino, California?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And what was it like during those early years of the 1900s in that part of the valley?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I always felt that it was the greatest place in the world, but it all changed.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Before smog; right?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How many people in your family?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I have three -- I had three brothers. My older brother has passed on.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And what did your father do for a living?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: That's a good question. He left us when we were very young.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So your mom raised you?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And what did she do for a living?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Believe it or not, she supported three growing boys working in a laundry.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And did you live in the same town all of your growing up years?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: When I was in the fifth grade we moved from San Bernardino to Pomona, California, and there -- I did my growing up there.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And did your mom continue to work in the same laundry then?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, after we got there.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did you boys have jobs too?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No. Occasionally, but it was the Depression, there weren't many jobs to be found.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What do you remember about the Depression?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Getting hungry.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were there a lot of people moving into the valley there?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: They were coming there from the Dust Bowl areas.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So you remember being hungry then?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What did you like to do in high school?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: The only reason I stayed in school is because I loved to play baseball and football and that's why I was in school.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So did you graduate from high school?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, and then I went on to college.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What year did you graduate from high school?

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: 1936. And then where did you go to college?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I went to Pomona Junior College. Graduated from there and went to La Verne College and graduated from there.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What was your interest in college?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Baseball and football.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Any academic interests?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, I was a very poor student.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: But you did play ball there?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Where were you and your family on December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: We were in Pomona. I can remember I was with friends and we were listening to the radio, I believe, and we heard that the Japanese had bombed Pearl Harbor. And I told my friends then I was going the next day to March Field and enlist, which I did.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Had there been any warning? Did anyone have a sense that this was coming to our country?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Not that I know of. I knew there was some kind of negotiations going on between the Japanese and our government, but I don't -- I don't know the outcome or what really went on with it.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How old were you then? You were in your early 20s, maybe?

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Had you already graduated from college?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, I was still in college. It took me a long time to get through college.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: The good old GI bill.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What about your brothers? Did they also enlist?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, my older brother was in the Navy. My younger brother also in the Air Corps

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What did your mom have to say about all of this?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: She took it like a trouper. She was a great woman.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Sounds like it. Did you see a radical change in the home front after the attack?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were people really -- in what way?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: People who you didn't expect to be too patriotic turned very patriotic.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Had you heard anything about Charles Lindbergh --

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: -- and his sense of not wanting our country to go to war? Norman C. Adams. Oh, no, I knew nothing of that.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Just that he was a great aviator, which he was.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did you want to fly as a kid? Did you have an interest in airplanes?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: The junior college I went to had a program where they -- you could -- how do I put it -- they were training pilots. Put it that way. And you could get into that program, and a lot of my friends did and went on from there into the Air Corps. When I went in the Air Corps, I didn't want anything to do with the fighting on the ground in the mud and all that.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So it wasn't out of a passion for flying?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: It's because you chose to be in the Air Corps rather than the Army.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did your mother say anything about her three boys going to war, leaving to go to war and she was left alone then at that point?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. No she didn't say.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Because of patriotism?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did she continue to work through the war years?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Okay. So you decided to join the Army Air Corps. And where did you do that?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: March Air Force Base in Riverside, California.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were there a lot of young men there enlisting at the time?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. Yes, to get into the cadet program you had to take a test and then they gave you the physical and then they interviewed you. After the interview, you found out whether you were accepted into the cadet program.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And were you accepted right away?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were any of your friends accepted with you?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, I had friends who were already commissioned and flying in the Air Corps. But when I went in there, I was by myself.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What about your brother? When did he enlist?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: My younger brother went in the Air Corps must have been about two years after I did.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So he didn't go in with you?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And so now you're accepted in the Army Air Corps and tell us about where you went from there. A whole new life.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Okay. They scheduled me to go to primary applied training in Phoenix, Arizona -- this is just my memory -- seems like about a month after I was enlisted and signed. And in the meantime the Air Corps changed their policy and they opened up -- one of the bases was Santa Ana, California, where whole -- all the cadets had to go through there. So instead of going to primary they sent me to Santa Ana and I was there for, I don't know, maybe three months. And then I went to primary, still at Phoenix. And like a lot of guys, I washed out of pilot training. And I asked what is the fastest way that I can get a commission? You could either volunteer to go into navigation training or bombardier training, and they said bombardier training is three or four months shorter. And I said: That's for me. And so that's what I did. And I went from there to New Mexico.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So they sent you to New Mexico for the bombardier training?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: And I graduated from bombardiers training on the 30th of December, '42, it would be.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Had you heard about the Norden bombsight at that point?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: That's what -- I used it all the time I was training.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: That's what you were training, really. What did you think about it?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. It was a super piece of machinery.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: If you learned how to use it, it was almost impossible to miss your target. Well, when I -- when I finished school, I don't know many bombs you dropped. But see I'm brand-new at this, never did it before in my life. Never saw a Norden bombsight except at the school. And my circular error was under 100 feet for all the bombs I dropped. So.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: You remember it being a closely guarded secret piece of equipment?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes, even in school you had to personally check the sight out, take it to the airplane, and bring it back and check in back in. Nobody was to help you; it was you alone. You would sign for it and it was your baby until you brought it back.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Uh-huh. How long were you in New Mexico then for the training?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: It took about seven, maybe eight months. And then I graduated.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And where'd you go from there?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I went from there to Tucson, Arizona, to Davis-Monthan Air Force Base.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Is that were you were assigned? Your group?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: They formed crews there and that's where I joined my B-24 crew.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: And then they sent -- after you were put on a crew, they formed training groups that went from Alamogordo, New Mexico, to another place in New Mexico. I can't think of the name of it. And then they declared your crew combat ready. And we were sent home supposedly -- well, it was for two-weeks leave and then we went back to Topeka, Kansas, picked up a B-24 as a crew, flew it from there to England.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were you with other B-24s? Norman C. Adams. No.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: By yourselves?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Individually.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were you ready to go into combat?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Time to go.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: That's why I joined.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What did you do the two weeks you were home?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, spent time with my mother.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: She knew you were going into combat?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. And I got married.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Okay. Was this a lady that you had known for a while?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, I'd known her for ever since we were little kids, practically. Although we had never -- until just before I went in the cadets, we dated a few times. And then when I went home on leave, I -- we decided it was a good time to get married.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What was her name?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Her name was Joella Woods. She was from Idaho originally. She grew up in Beulah.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Small world.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So off you all went to England by yourself, a sole B-24 with a crew?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Where did you land? Can you show us on the map where you actually came into England?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I -- let's see.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: You went by way of what, Greenland?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. Let's see if I can -- it doesn't show Greenland, does it? Let's see if I can find it. First we landed up here by Edinburgh. And there was base there where they took the new airplanes in and modified them. So we left our airplane there and rode on a train down the first night in England. The train went through London and I said I may never go back here again, so I'm going to stay here tonight. And I did. I should have stayed with my crew, but I didn't. I was a nonconformer, I guess. And then our base, let's see -- it was up here. They called this little place the Wash. Our base was close to it. I don't see the name of that town here. And then when we got there they said that our group wouldn't be -- our crew wouldn't be flying any missions out of England; that we were going to start low-level training.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What does that mean?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: That was for the Ploiesti raids, is what that meant. We thought that's what it meant, but we weren't sure. But we flew low-level missions around England just above trees. And then they -- let's see, I think it was in May.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And this would be 2003 now -- I'm sorry, 1943?

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: 1943, okay.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, we went to North Africa and we flew some missions out of Benghazi up into -- in the desert there, Benghazi, flew up into Italy. And -- I think our crew flew four missions, the most notable was when we bombed Rome. Where is Rome? I don't see it.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What were you bombing in Rome?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: We bombed the marshalling yards. All the rails in Italy came through Rome, so we bombed the marshalling yards.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Would you go in with two or three other airplanes or with a fighter escort?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I never saw a fighter escort, no. Our whole group flew. So we would be, say, 30 aircraft in formation. And --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What was it like using the Norden bombsight the first time in real combat? Out of the classroom; the real thing?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: See, that's what's funny about it. You always train and flying in formation and you didn't have to use the bombsight for what it's made for. You dropped -- when the leader dropped his bombs, you dropped yours. So he was doing the -- our crew was never a lead crew. So --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So you never really used what you learned?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did you get a lot of flak? What did you have?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did you have fighters attacking you or was it mostly flak?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: A lot of flak. And on one mission, I think our crew shot down the first jet aircraft in Europe. I think.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I saw this fighter coming at us and no propeller and I thought that's a funny airplane. And our top gunner shot him down. I know he did. We saw him explode.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: That would have been the Me262. That was the German --

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I don't know what it was.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Wow. So you were pretty shocked when you saw that?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes, I couldn't believe what I was seeing. An airplane with no propeller?

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did it appear to be going very fast?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes. A lot faster than you normally saw.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What was it like being in combat maybe the first time?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I guess I'm funny, but it really didn't bother me. I was -- I always felt that nothing was ever going to happen to our crew, and I guess it kept me from worrying about it. A lot of guys went nuts worrying about getting shot down. But --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Tell us about when you were shot down. Tell us about what happened. You were going into Rumania; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, yes. I should have brought that book for you -- to let you have it here -- that tells about the mission. In the first place, it was well planned.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What was the mission?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: The bombing of oil fields in Rumania at low level. And the first thing went wrong was when you're flying a bombing mission you have an initial point where you turn to go to the target. Well, the guy -- the crew that was leading the mission made the wrong turn and picked out the wrong initial point and we turned too soon. And we were supposed to bomb, I think it was, from the west to the east. And the way he turned made us bomb from the east to the west.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Can you show us Rumania on the map where you were bombing?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Where is Ploiesti? I can't find it.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: But that's the general area?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, here is Bucharest. Ploiesti was north of Bucharest up in here somewhere.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Okay. So he turned the wrong direction?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, see the initial point was supposed to take us -- let's see, we came up here this way. The initial point was supposed to take us this way at the target. Well, we went clear to Bucharest, then turned north, and then back to the target and it screwed up the whole mission.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What happened?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: But -- well, one -- the group behind us flew the mission as planned. So we're going from the east to the west; they're coming at us from the west to the east. So this way on the target. It was not very pleasant.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Was there a name for this mission?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Just -- yes, the Tidal Wave.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And so was there a lot of -- a lot of gunfire going on, or flak?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes. That wrong turn took us right up a railroad track -- about 30 miles of a railroad track, which was probably the most heavily fortified 30 miles in Europe. And we're flying treetop level. They could have thrown rocks at us and hit us. And we got shot up pretty bad. We lost -- let's see, the Number Two engine. Then we lost the Number Four -- no, Two and Three -- and there wasn't enough power to keep us airborne. We dropped the bombs and made it out of the target area and crash-landed in the cornfield. And luckily -- the safest place, supposedly, in the B-24 is up on the flight deck where the pilots and the radar were. And the nose was the worst place you could be. The navigator and I, we never got out of the nose. We were in the nose when we hit the ground. But luckily --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What were you thinking?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I thought this was it. I really did. You know, they talk about seeing the light at the end of the tunnel. Well, I saw that light. But luckily --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Was it a glass nose?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Plexiglass.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Plexiglass. And you saw it all through the nose?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah. And we were lucky. I don't know -- they had dug a trench across that field and there was a mound of dirt. And when we landed, it was a pretty good crash landing for what had gone on. And before we had hit the ground, we hit the mound of dirt and it broke the nose off and I was in it and it rolled on ahead of the airplane.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were you knocked out at all?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, I came to feeling heat and I thought: This thing's on fire. I better get out of here. And then I realized I wasn't in the airplane; I was in what was left of the nose. And I got untangled from all the stuff that was in there and got out. And by then the airplane -- what was left of it -- was completely engulfed in flame. And I started to run to get away from there. And then I thought, well, somebody else might want to get out of this thing. And so I went back and I helped our engineer, helped him out of it and away from the airplane. And I helped one of the gunners who, incidentally, both of them died from burns that first night, so my effort was in vain. But at least I did it. And --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did the navigator make it through because of you?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No. During our fight to the target, I think it was a 20-millimeter shell came up through -- as far as I could figure went between my legs and hit the navigator somewhere in the chest and he was in bad shape. And I said, "David, I can't do anything for you until I drop these bombs. Why don't you try to get up to the flight deck." And I don't think he ever made it and I think he was probably -- there's a little kind of -- it wasn't a tunnel, it was a hole that you went up from the flight deck to get from the nose. And I think he was in there when it hit the ground. So whatever happened, I don't know. I know he got killed.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What about the pilot and the copilot?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: They both got out. And we got one gunner out. Out of ten people, four of us got out alive.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Any other airplanes in the group go down too?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes. Our group sent -- oh, let's see, I think our group sent 28 aircraft and they got two got back.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Because of the wrong turn?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, that's -- I don't know whether anybody will ever admit this, but the wrong turn -- that group, the lead group, they didn't even go to the target. They flew around it. Our group flew to the target. That group didn't lose any airplanes. We lost -- well, not all shot down, but got back to Benghazi that night with two of our aircraft. Some of them were in Bulgaria; some of them were in Turkey. They were all over the place. And there were quite of few of us on the ground too.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So after you got out of the plane, and the pilot and the copilot and one of the gunners, did you all get to stay together?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I thought I was the only one out of the airplane, except the two guys that got away from it. And then we landed in this cornfield and not too far away -- I would say must have been 100, maybe 200 yards away from this was a gun emplacement. German. And before I could really do anything for those two guys when I got out of the airplane, this German had a bayonet and was pushing me off towards -- so I sat in the gun revetment and watched him shoot up B-24s.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How awful.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Nothing you could do.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah, and then also shortly after I got in the gun revetment, they brought our little waist gunner and so I knew there was two of us alive. So we sat there. And then they kind of settled down. They took us to a building, and I don't know what building or anything else. But they assembled all of the guys that survived on the ground and then I saw my two pilots.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How many were there? How many survived that raid?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: There were 110 of us.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were you wounded?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I had some flak in my left leg and in my hands. And I don't know whether it was flak or just smoke or something from that shell that went off in the nose, but my face was all black. And little things for years kept coming out of my skin -- I don't know what it was -- and my hands.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So over 110 of you then were detained there in that one spot?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Okay. What then happened?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: They moved us from there, from Ploiesti down to Bucharest to a school house, I think it was. They kept us there for a while. And then they moved us back into the mountains, the Carpathian Mountains to a little town called Timisoara de sus. They made a prison camp up there. 110 of us we were kept there.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were you the only ones there?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: They didn't bring from other -- Australia or England?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, there was two civilians from England who had been captured in Germany when the war broke out and the Germans had detained them. They escaped and got all the way to Rumania and they got caught again. So they stuck them with us. And then there were three Russians who were -- let's see, they were captured when the -- when the -- when the Germans went into Russia --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: -- these three were captured. And why they brought them to Rumania, I don't know, but they put them in our camp. And there was one -- I think he was a Bulgarian pilot that was in our camp. And that was it.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did your family know that you were prison of war? Or how long before your mother knew?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: She -- they got a Missing in Action wire shortly after the mission. And then it was about three months before they knew that I was a POW.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What was your state of mind? It must have been surreal in the beginning when you were first captured and the plane was gone.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: It was, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: It was shock probably. And then --

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Again, I knew I was going to get out of it okay, and it didn't bother me. But our copilot, he was -- he just went out of his mind. He was frantic. But when we finally got loose, he was all right. But he just was a worrier, I guess. But most of the guys in the camp were very good.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What was camp life like? Because that's a small camp. You were in a really small prisoner of war camp. What was it like? You were there for 14 months; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What was it like?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: What it was, it was in a retirement area for the railroad workers of Rumania. Then they took it over and put barbed wire fences and the whole deal around it. The building itself wasn't bad.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How were you treated?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Good, except we -- so, the Germans turned us over to the Rumanians. So the Rumanians were guarding us and there were more guards than there were prisoners. But we ate the same food that the guards ate. And we got hungry at times, but.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did you ever see any American airplanes come over?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Tell us about that.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I remember being outside of the building and we heard this noise that you can't miss. And sure enough, I can't remember if they were '70s or '24s at high altitude. There was an oil field that was to our east or north of where we were, and that was also a target and that's where they were going.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How you did feel when you saw them fly over?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: You knew they were still in the war.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah, and they rushed us back in the building. They didn't want us -- but that only happened one time.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were you ever interrogated about the Norden bombsight? Did they know you were a bombardier and that you had that information, that you had that knowledge?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, but they didn't -- what amazed me about the Germans when they interrogated me, they knew my whole life practically. They knew especially the part of my life that was in the military. They knew where I graduated, when I graduated, what I graduated as. It was amazing. So their intelligence was probably a lot better than ours.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: When it came time -- did you have any sense that the war was coming to an end?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: That we were winning? How did you -- why?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: They would bring us -- about once a month they would bring a barber in if you wanted to get a haircut or whatever. And he smuggled a little radio -- smuggled a little radio into camp and we hid it down in the basement. And we couldn't all go down there, but one or two guys would go down and listen to it. And we knew when D-Day happened. And I told them that happened because that's my birthday.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How did you feel on that day, on D-Day?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Great. Great, because we knew it wouldn't be long then.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Well, tell us about the liberation of your camp.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Okay. We come up one morning and no guards. And we thought: This is strange. Then the Rumanian captain who was the Commandant of the camp came and told us that the Germans all were pulling out and we were free. And we said: Well, we're free. What do we do now? And like I said, there were more guards than there were prisoners. They were going to move the guards somewhere and I forget how many trucks they had. But we said, well -- and we knew there were quite a few prisoners down in Bucharest, the capital, who had been shot down on high-level raids that came after us. And we knew there were more than 110 of them. We figured that if our government was going to do anything for anybody it would be for them, because of the accessibility and the numbers. And so we said: We've got to get to Bucharest. And so we told the Rumanians: Well, I don't know how many trucks you've got, but I think we took four to get our 110 guys aboard and headed for Bucharest.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How did that feel to be free after 14 months?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: It was good. But still, very happy -- what do we do now?

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Because no one knew you were there, did they?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: The U.S. Government didn't know you were there?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: They didn't know where we were. That's right. Anyway, we were going down this highway, the German army that's pulling out is going one way and we were going the other way on the same highway. And then the Rumanians, before we got to Bucharest, the Rumanians decided they were going to declare war on Germany. So now there is a war going on between where we are and where we wanted to go. So we stayed -- and I think we stayed three days in a little town. The people took us in and were real great to us. And we stayed there for, I think, three days, until that war went by us, or whatever. We had a clear shot to Bucharest. We got to Bucharest, I think it was, on a Sunday afternoon. And the next morning, B-17s from Italy were flown in to take us out of there. So we just -- we just made it.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And where did they fly you to?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Back to Italy.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Back to Italy. And then when did you get to come home?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, that's another story. There was one character in the camp -- he was the ranking officer, he was a major -- who collaborated with the Rumanians and the Germans. And so some way our government knew about it.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did you know about it when you were in the camp? Norman C. Adams. Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: You guys knew it?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What did you think of him?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Not very much.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did he live among you?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. Anyway, they took -- they took the two pilots, myself, and I don't know, must have been ten other guys back to England from Italy to court-martial -- to stand by to testify in a court-martial for this guy.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Was he convicted? Norman C. Adams. Yes, but he got a slap on the wrist. He was discharged without honor, which is nothing.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: No time in jail?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And after that, now did your mom know at this point that you had been liberated?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Had the Red Cross brought anything in? Did the Red Cross even know you all were there?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: We got Red Cross packages one time. But I think maybe there had been more, but I think the Rumanians took them. I'm not sure; this is just my guess.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So from England, you came back to the United States?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And where did you come to? Where did they bring you?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Washington, D.C.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How did that feel when you landed on American soil?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Great. Great. And they interrogated us quite extensively for a couple of days

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: About what? What did they want to know?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: What had gone on and also about this court-martial. And then they sent us home.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What was that like when you got home?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, great, great. My younger brother was there. He was in Cadets in Victorville, California, which is just right close to where we lived. And he was home when -- when I got home. Sue Paul; What about your older brother in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: He was in the Navy. I don't know where he was. In fact, I didn't see my older brother until after the war.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So this was in 1945, and you decide to stay in --

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, Christmas of '44.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Christmas of '44. And then stayed in the United States then?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. Yes, that was one thing. Having been a POW, they weren't gonna send us -- wouldn't send us to any -- well, I thought they might send me to the Pacific, but they just wouldn't. They said no.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Had there been any rumors of this incredible bomb that we had?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What had you heard about that?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Just how awesome it was.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Where were you stationed at this point?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I think it was Midland, Texas.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Is that where you were when the A-bomb was dropped?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, I think I was up in Victorville, California. That was when --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Is that where you were when VJ came?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. That was one thing about having been a POW, I could pick where I wanted to be. I wanted to go to March Air Force Base, but there was no place for me. So they sent me up to Victorville, which was all right. I could commute, almost, if I could get the gasoline.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Uh-huh. There wasn't much, was there?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So the home front was pretty patriotic and --

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: -- and a lot going on here, wasn't there:

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And you were with your wife then?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So you all settled in Victorville?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, she stayed in Pomona.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Oh, she did? Okay. Did you have any children at this point?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No. We never had any children.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Well, when the war ended, VJ Day came and our country, of course, was so ecstatic, the end of the war, what decisions did you make about your life and what you wanted to do at that point?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I already decided that I was going to stay in the service. See I -- I went to college thinking that I might -- I wanted to be a teacher and a coach. Coach is what I wanted to be. But to be a coach most of the time meant that you had to start out as a teacher. But then I decided -- I don't know what they call it now, but then they called it "practice teaching" and after one semester of it, I made up my mind that I would never be a teacher. I couldn't fight those kids. So I already made up my mind that I was going to stay in the service.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How did your wife feel about that?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: She was great. She was a good trouper.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So you stayed in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Is that when you went into the Fifteenth Air Force, the 22nd Bomb Group? Was it at that point that you were reassigned to that?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: But you stayed as a bombardier?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: That was still your --

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. There was -- the Air Force had a program they called -- I can't think what they called it. Anyway, what they wanted to do was take all bombardiers that were going to stay in the service to learn navigation and radar operation. So I -- and there was an age limit and I was approaching that age limit. So they -- they sent me to that school. And then when I got out of that school, I was assigned to Fairchild Air Force Base in Washington, and in B-36s.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Where were you when you saw your first jet and what did you think of it and what was it?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, the first one I saw, I know, was that fighter that our crew shot down.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Yeah, but we brought that technology here and we developed it --

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: -- successfully in other jets.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Out of B-36 and I went into the B-52. I was a navigator in a B-52 crew for a while.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And where were you stationed at that point?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I was at Fairchild Air Force Base. Went from there to Puerto Rico, still in B-36s. And B-36s in Puerto Rico we flew airborne alert between there and North Africa. And we carried -- well, SAC at that time was probably the biggest deterrent to the Russians. And every crew in SAC had a target assigned in Russia.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Was it a flip-over for you then to go from the Russians being our allies in the first war and now you're fighting the Russians?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: I mean, mentally you had to make that flip-over.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: You might say we were brainwashed about the Russians.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And so North Africa was your area?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, we were airborne alert. We flew -- were on alert from the time we took off in Puerto Rico until we landed in North Africa. And then we were on ground alert there, and then took off from there back and airborne halfway back to Puerto Rico. And we had the Big Mom on board.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: With the intent to drop it where? Norman C. Adams. At our assigned target. Every crew in SAC had an assigned target in Russia. And we practiced -- not the mission, but one that would simulate the mission if it would go. The bell rang and we were going to go. So --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Pretty intense.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah, it was. Got pretty tight at times.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Where were you during the Korean War, once Korea became --

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I was assigned to B-36s in Spokane. And again, I was lucky. See, that was our first line of aircraft in the Air Force, was the B-36, and they didn't send them to Korea. And then when Vietnam came along, I was in B-52s in the B-52Gs, which they did not send -- the earlier models, they did go to Vietnam, but the later models, they didn't. So I lucked out again.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How did you sense the change of tide in America of those three wars, World War II, Korea, Vietnam, the Cold War?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, I was always amazed that there was not more recognition of what those people had done, which was -- war is not a happy occurrence.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: But supporting our troops is a very important thing.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, that's right.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: In World War II, of course, we had such a height of patriotism and togetherness in this country.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, that's right.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Korea, there was kind of a nonchalant attitude.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Like it never happened.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: People wanting to have a life without war.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Although there was a great respect for our soldiers.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Then in Vietnam, of course, the whole country came unglued and it was a divisive moment in time.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I think what happened, especially in Vietnam, was like B-52s are sent over there and they were bombing bamboo bridges. Now, come on. We carried -- in a 52 you could get 30 bombs aboard to bomb bamboo bridges? Come on. We weren't in it to win. That was my opinion.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Well, we didn't win.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: And we bombed Hanoi one time and got their attention, but that was it.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: My gosh, your military history took in the three, you know, the most significant wars in the history of this country. Which leaders do you think the most highly of, of those? I mean, because you saw all the great leaders in those three. Do you have any that stood out in your mind that you thought the most of, or the least of? What are your -- give us some comments on that.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: I met Eisenhower when I got out of prison back to England, and I was tremendously impressed by him.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Why? Norman C. Adams. He just had something about him that you knew he was a great guy. Just --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: A good soldier?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah. And then, oh --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What about MacArthur? You never met him?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Or Patton?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, but he must have been something else. He must have been. And I'm sure the tales you hear are true. I have talked to and met guys who were in his outfit and the one thing you didn't want to do was bad-mouth Patton, because they would be all over you. And he's to be respected, to me anyway. He was from a wealthy family. He never collected a nickel of -- a nickel as a salary from the being in the Army. Not one nickel.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What about Claire Chennault? Did you ever hear anything about him?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, no, that's the other direction in the war. I never got in that direction.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: That didn't trickle down?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Now, your wife was able to travel with you then? She moved to the different parts of the U.S. with you?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And when did you decide to retire from the military?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, that is not a nice story. But I worked for a full colonel that I thought was impossible. I would have stayed for 30 years. I made the lieutenant colonel list, but at that time the way it worked you had to stay until -- depending on your majority date of rank, you were somewhere on the list. Because of that date, you didn't know whether you had to wait six months to a year or whatever. And if you put the promotion on, put the 30 days, on you were obligated for two more years in the service. By then, see, I had 26-and-a-half years and was working for -- excuse my language -- a complete idiot. And I just made up by mind I've got to get out of here before I do something that's not --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How long were you working under him?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: A year and-a-half.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And that's what made you decide to retire?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes. Yep.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So you put in for your retirement?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And you retired what as a -- you were --

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: A major, when I retired.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Major when you retired. Where were you based when you retired?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: In Maine. Northern Maine. Loring Air Force Base. The end of the world.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And what did you and your wife decide that you were going to do once you retired?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, I knew what I wanted to do, and she would go along with anything I wanted to do. Of course, if she wanted to do something she could do it. But I always liked golf as a disease. Hunting and fishing came very close. And I had come -- when I was in Spokane, I'd come down and visit her cousin --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: In Idaho?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: In Idaho -- and go pheasant hunting with him. And I made up my mind -- that was a long time -- I made up my mind this is where I wanted to retire, was in Idaho. And my wife said that she didn't really want to come back to Idaho. But she said: As long as we are going to retire in Idaho, it's going to be Nampa, because that's where I have my cousin and my aunt and uncle live in Emmett, so and at least I'll know someone. And I said: Fine with me. And that's how I got here.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What year did you move here?

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And did you stay retired then?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And you fished and hunted and played golf?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: That's all I've done since I got out of the service, until I had the stroke. And now I don't do anything. After I retired, my wife was diagnosed with cancer and she died about four months later. And we had -- we had moved to Nampa. And when she got sick, I took her back to California and took her to the Naval Hospital. That's where she was diagnosed with cancer and then died shortly thereafter. And so I came back to Nampa and I had been to a dentist here in Nampa and talked -- had talked to his receptionist several times. And I don't know how the subject -- the subject came up and I told her that my wife had died. And she said: I have a real good friend I think you should meet. And I wanted to know why and she told me that she also -- she had lost her mate and maybe we'd be good for each other. And I didn't know whether that was a good idea or not. And I kind of kicked it around and kept telling her: I don't think so, I don't think so. And finally, the next time I went in she brought the subject up again and so I said: Okay. I'll meet her. So I met the woman and about year and-a-half later, we were married. I married a family. My first wife and I had no children. Wilma had four and she wasn't too sure whether I could handle four kids or not. But I immediately liked all of them, and especially her, and we have gotten along great. And right at first, the two youngest weren't too sure about this new dad. But the two oldest accepted me right off and were great. And then eventually the two young ones came around and we've been a great family ever since.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Do you have any grandchildren?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: We have ten grandchildren and three great grandchildren.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So a big family?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: A great family.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Uh-huh. It's a blessing you survived in the nose of that B-24 knocked off, but you walked away from that so you could have this experience in your life with this family. The Norden bombsight was one of the most highly classified secrets of World War II and you had the opportunity to train on it and then to use it. Could you tell us what was so special about this bombsight?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: What was special about it? Well, the first thing, if you knew how to use it -- there was no way you could ever really miss your target, if you knew how to use it and used it properly. Plus it helped in navigation, because it would give the navigator wind and drift readings that he needs for his navigation.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did the navigator in the plane use it also though?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, not --

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Or did the bombardier give him information?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, the bombardier gave him the information he needed off of it.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Tell us a little bit about your training, how were you trained to use it?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, first, when you first went to bombardier school, they put you on a trainer which amounted to kind of a scaffolding -- a scaffolding on wheels. The bombsight was mounted on at scaffolding on wheels. And on the floor they had -- the school I went to they had pennies on the floor they used it as a target. And the instructor was sitting with you and explaining what to do, how to use the sight. And my instructor was -- I thought -- super, because he taught me things that weren't really in the book on how to use it. And the knobs on it kills your ground speed and wind direction which causes drift, you kill that, it relays it to the autopilot, and it corrects the aircraft to fly where this thing tells you to fly.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: You actually hook the airplane up to this Norden bombsight?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So at some point the plane is turned over to this other person.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: You're flying the airplane. The bombmen, you're flying the airplane with the bombsight.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: How far out from the target is the plane turned over to you?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, depending on the target -- there's a thing on this called extended vision. You can run the telescope out to where you can see maybe 40 miles. And then you -- at 40 miles all you're doing is making sure you're killing all the drift so that you're on track to the target. And then at a certain point the crosshairs will get to the target. And then you clutch them in and then with a couple of other knobs you kill the ground speed, which that information goes into the bombsight and tells it when to drop the bombs.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: It's not computer driven?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Because we didn't have computers then.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, no. It's all inside of that thing.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: You know, there's been rumor forever actually that I've always heard that this -- that the crosshair, one the secrets of the Norden bombsight is the crosshair is from a spiderweb. Is that true?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: That's what we were told, so I guess it's true.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Amazing. So did you feel when you went into combat pretty good knowing that you had this incredible piece of equipment?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Were you told that the Germans wanted them?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes, they had nothing that would compare to this. As far as that goes, the Germans missed the boat anyway. They didn't have any heavy bombardment.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What kind of security surrounded the Norden bombsights, both on the bases and once they were in the airplanes? Norman C. Adams. On the base, they were in a safe. Always. And when you were going to use it in training, and also in combat, the bombardier checked it out, signed for it, took it to the aircraft, installed it, the head of it. This section here was always in the airplane, but the secret part is the top of this bombsight. Something really interesting, there's gyroscopes in the head and in the stabilizer. I forget the RPMs, but it's unreal how fast those gyroscopes are turning. In fact, if you took the head off of the stabilizer before that thing slowed down it could almost throw you on the ground, the torque from the little gyroscope. Well, you can see it. That knob on top is what cages the gyroscope. In other words, it's got a stem that sticks up and that fits over so that the gyroscope won't tumble in all directions.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Did you set it before you left?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: Knowing what your coordinates were, you would set it before you took off?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: No, now this has nothing to do with where you are. What you had to know is what altitude you were going to be flying at and what air speed you were going to be flying at. That's all the bombardier needed to know. When you went into some charts there were -- told you air speed and altitude, told you where to set your disk speed, which converted into ground speed after using the site.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: What happened to yours when you all crashed? Norman C. Adams. On that mission we didn't have one on board. So we were flying low-level. What you could do, you could use them at low-level, but it wasn't that efficient at low-level. It was strictly a high-level piece of equipment. This shows approach to the target of B-24s. This smoke -- (Indicating on photograph) -- they have smoke towers all the way around the target so that they made visibility poor so you couldn't see where your target was. And let's see, here is another picture of it. You can see how low we were. See these towers, that was the cracking plants that produced what was high-octane gasoline. That's what we were bombing. Not the oil fields itself. The refineries is what we were after.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: So is this -- is this actually -- are these pictures of where you were?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yeah, that's an actual picture. That's an actual picture.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And that's of your group?

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Well, I don't know if it was our group. This here makes me think that was -- in fact, I know it was the 98th bomb group which was stationed in North Africa. He was -- the commander of the 98th, Colonel Kane, quite a guy.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: That's quite an airplane, the B-24.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: It got no recognition. I don't know what else to say about that.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: That's great. That's great. Well, my gosh, I have to say to you that this has been an incredible interview. The life that you have had is incredible. You know, from coming from a single-parent family environment with a mom who worked her heart out and you obviously loved and respected tremendously.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And then the greatest war that this world has ever known, you went into that and served so valiantly in the Air Corps and became a prisoner of war, and survived that. Obviously, you were meant to live a long life. Because it's almost a miracle that you have survived what you did.

sp.speaker: Norman C. Adams
sp.p: Long life. That's something that I've said for a long time. When I was in high school if somebody told me I was going to live to be 88 years old, I'd say you've got a screw loose.

sp.speaker: Sue Paul
sp.p: And I tell you, you look like you're 70, so whatever you're doing you're doing well. And then you had a long, distinguished career in the military. And I want to tell you that we are so proud to have you here. And we want to thank you so much for being an American veteran. This country is what it is today because of men like you. And we value so much.
